Breadboard rows follow the catalogue naming (bank 't' = rows a-e). The lower rail pair is used: 'bn' is the ground rail and 'bp' is the 5V rail. The rail hole numbers are approximate.

The E8 warning is not a real problem for this manual, so the graph is unchanged from my previous answer. The buzzer legs sit in columns 26 and 30 of the bottom bank. The A0 wire lands in column 26, the signal side, so I used pin 2 (+) there. The black jumper in column 30 goes to the ground rail, so pin 1 (-) is there.
Rail hole numbers are estimated from the image. The bottom rail's upper row is the black-marked negative rail (bn) and its lower row is the red-marked positive rail (bp).
The buzzer is driven directly from the DAC pin with no series resistor, as in the tutorial image.

The two 18650 cells sit in the holder in series: cell1 + goes to the holder positive lead, cell1 - goes to cell2 +, and cell2 - goes to the holder negative lead. This is an assumption.

Circuit: D9 -> red wire -> R1 (220 ohm) -> LED anode; LED cathode -> black wire -> GND. This matches the schematic.

The breadboard is drawn rotated in the image. The strip names 8t, 9t and 10t are my choice of columns. The wire end is in row a and the sensor leg in row e of each strip.

Parts are unchanged from step 1.
The Due's ground port is named GND on arduino-due-r3, not GND.1, so the shield's GND edge now uses GND.

The motor leads go into the shield's channel A screw terminals. A lead into a screw terminal is not a compatible join pair, so these two connections are electrical edges only, with no joined edge. Which lead goes to + or - decides the 'forward' direction, and the manual doesn't say.

The arduino-due-r3 type has no 'power-jack' or 'usb-micro' port. The wall wart's DC plug is therefore a port-less joined edge to the Due, and its tip is wired electrically to the Due's VIN, which the DC jack feeds.
The USB cable has no catalogue ports, so its joined edge to the Due has no ports.
Parts are unchanged from step 1 (no breadboard; 7 jumper wires: 5 blue signal, 1 red 3.3V, 1 black GND).

Wiring the SCP1000 3.3V and GND pins straight to the board's 3.3V and GND headers is what the tutorial shows. The sensor is a breakout module with no LED or other load, so nothing needs to sit between the wire and the supply pin. This E2 finding is not a real problem for this build.

The shield sits on the Uno, so its top sockets carry the Uno's signals (the 'conducts' groups tie each socket to its stacking pin). The jumper wires plug into the shield's top sockets, as in the image.
The shield's rj45 port is typed header-socket so the Ethernet cable's lead end fits it. The cable's other end goes to the network, which is not a part in the graph.
The schematic crosses D7/D6 on purpose. D7 goes to CSB and D6 to DRDY, matching the text, code and image.

SPI wiring follows the code comment and the Uno's real SPI pins: D13 to SCK, D11 to MOSI, D12 to MISO. The labels in the schematic and the image's wire ends are hard to read and look swapped, so I used the electrically correct mapping.

I could not read the right-hand end of the green jumper on row C from the image. I put it at column 15, the IN1- pin, because the schematic needs IN1- tied to the R10/R11 junction. Column 14 would short the output to the inverting input.

The 100 nF capacitor uses the generic non-polar capacitor-22pf type with value=100nF, because the catalogue has no 100 nF type.

Current path: D2, then resistor, then LED anode, then LED cathode, then GND. This matches the schematic.

Not a real problem, so the graph is unchanged: the [E8] 'needs at least 7.0 V but 3V3 is on 3.3 V' warning treats the Due's 3V3 pin as a supply input. Parts are the same as step 1 except that both boards now use a new type, arduino-mkr-wan-1300-pins. The pushbutton now sits across the centre gap, as its card requires. Top half (image top block, bank 'b'): 1.l in column 5 and 2.l in column 7. The breadboard images label the top block rows j-f and the bottom block e-a, which is the reverse of the catalogue's naming. The image's top block is therefore written as bank 'b' (rows f-j), and the bottom block as bank 't' (rows a-e). Row f is next to the centre gap.

Each antenna connects to its board through its own cable. The board type has no antenna port, so that edge has no port on the board side.

Receiver: pin 2 goes through the green wire and the resistor to the LED anode. The LED cathode goes through the black wire to GND. The LED's bent (longer) leg in the image is taken as the anode. The resistor is on the anode side as the image shows.

The 5 V vs 3.3 V warning came from the VCC edge I removed. Nothing now puts 5 V on the shield's 3.3 V-rated VCC. The MKR board runs at 3.3 V logic, and the shield's low-power side is 3.3 V.
The tutorial says any MKR family board; I used the MKR WiFi 1010 (arduino-mkr1000-wifi).
The relays are wired inside the shield to MKR pins 1 and 2, so there are no wires for them.

The circuit image was not available, so the LED wiring is my assumption. Pin 3 goes through a jumper wire to LED_1's anode. Its cathode goes through a 220 ohm resistor to the breadboard ground rail. Pin 4 does the same for LED_2. One jumper wire takes MKR GND to the ground rail.
Resistor value (220 ohm) and LED colours are assumed, as the tutorial doesn't give them.
The 24V supply and 24V lamp on the high-power terminals are only an illustrative example, so I did not build them.

Fix: the carrier's screw-terminal ports (VIN, GND, M1+..M4-) were kind 'lug', which does not pair with a lead. They are now kind 'header-socket', because a bare lead or wire end is clamped into each terminal, and lead into header-socket is a compatible join. The connections are unchanged.
MKR Motor Carrier is not in the catalogue (lookup_part only found the different MKR Connector Carrier), so a new type was drafted.

The MKR family board is unspecified; the image resembles a MKR WiFi 1010, so arduino-mkr1000-wifi was used. It plugs into the carrier's MKR socket via its header pins, so the edge to the board has no board-side port.
The 3S LiPo battery's leads go to the VIN/GND terminal block on the carrier (screw terminals); no jumper wires or breadboard are used.
The optional DC motor is wired to M1+/M1- as in the circuit image; its leads are symmetric, so lead 1 to M1+ is arbitrary.
The carrier's ON/OFF switch is not modelled as a part; the tutorial says to flick it to ON.
The optional power supply is an alternative to the battery and is not included.

The carrier catalogue entry has no ports. Earlier, null-port electrical edges to it merged supply, ground and signals into one node, which caused the short. The carrier now has only physical (joined) edges, and its pass-through wiring is modelled as electrical edges from the MKR Zero pins to the Grove cable pins (A1 = SIG/SCL, A2 = SDA, A3 = VCC 3.3V, A4 = GND). The MKR Zero sits on the carrier's headers, so this is equivalent.

The 12V supply's tip (+) goes to the carrier's VIN screw terminal, shown as electrical to wire3, which feeds relay COM. The supply sleeve (GND) is tied to the MKR Zero GND, which is the carrier's GND. The carrier's 12V-to-board regulation is internal and not modelled.
I removed the earlier edges putting the 12V supply directly on the MKR Zero VIN. The carrier's regulator sits between them, and the MKR VIN pin is not 12V-rated.
I dropped the two wires to the supply, because a wire-end can't join the barrel-jack tip/sleeve sockets. The supply is assumed to have stripped leads screwed into the carrier terminals.
The 12V power schematic image wasn't provided. I assumed the usual wiring: 12V+ to relay COM, relay NO to pump +, pump - to GND.
The Arduino MKR Zero wasn't found by lookup_part, so it is a new part type. Its I2C pins are D11 (SDA) and D12 (SCL).
The two solid wires are soldered to two unconnected tinned bars of the water sensor. The sensor has no port for individual bars, so those edges use null ports.
The Grove relay's NC_CONTACT is unused. The MKR Zero is powered over USB for programming.
The six Grove cables are my addition to the manual's parts list. The vase and plant are left out.

Port-kind fixes: the catalogue's Grove cable (grove-cable-4pin-f) has socket-kind ports, which cannot join the carrier's Grove header or the sensor's pins. It is replaced by a new type, grove-cable-4pin-grove, with the same 8 port names and through pairs (A1-B1 and so on) but pin-hole ports. Pin into pin-hole is a valid pair, and the carrier's A6 Grove connector and the sensor pins are pins.
The carrier's relay terminals are now header-socket kind, so the pump's lead and the USB cable's wire-end are valid joins into them. In reality they are screw terminals that clamp a wire.
The open-ended USB cable's usb-a plug is kind ball, which pairs with the adapter's socket-kind USB-A port (a plug-into-receptacle join). This is a stand-in, because no USB-specific kind exists.

The carrier has a single A6 port for the Grove connector, so the Grove cable's four conductors are shown as one connection from grove1 A1 to carrier A6. The sensor end is wired pin by pin (B1 SIG, B2 NC, B3 VCC, B4 GND).
The pump is wired as the tutorial says: open-ended cable positive to relay 1 NO, pump positive (port 1, the supply side) to relay 1 COM, and the cable negative joined to the pump negative (port 2).
The usb-power-adapter type has only one USB-A port (A), so both USB cables go to port A as a simplification. The tutorial says the adapter has at least 2 USB ports.
Relay 1 is the one used in the circuit text, although the code drives opla.Relay2. The circuit text and image take priority, so relay 1 is wired.
The watering pipe, water container and optional connector strip are left out because they are not electronic parts. No breadboard or jumper wires are used.
Parts are unchanged from step 1.
Each Opta's USB-C port goes by a USB-C cable to the computer running PLC IDE (as in the diagram), and its ETH RJ-45 port goes by an RJ-45 cable to the Ethernet switch.

The checker flagged the joined edges between an RJ-45 cable end (lead) and the Opta ETH port (kind socket). I misread which edges these were last time and changed the electrical ones instead. The catalogue gives the Opta's ETH port a kind that does not pair with a lead, and I can't change a catalogue port. The cable really does plug into the Opta's RJ-45 socket, so I kept the joined edge but named no port on the Opta side. The electrical edges name the ETH port and were not flagged.
The Ethernet switch is the recommended set-up; without it a single RJ-45 cable could join the two Opta devices directly.
The optional 'Modbus TCP Compatible Device' box in the diagram is omitted because it is not in the parts list.
usb-cable has no ports in the catalogue, so USB edges use null for the cable's port.
The computer is not in the hardware list; it is kept because the USB-C cables need an endpoint and the diagram shows it.
Step 1 parts are unchanged: Arduino UNO, servo, and three jumper wires (no breadboard, as the circuit image shows the servo wired straight to the UNO).
Connections follow the circuit image and text: servo PWR (red) to 5V, servo GND (black) to GND, servo signal to digital pin 9, which matches myservo.attach(9).

The image shows the black wire going to a GND pin in the power header, next to 5V. The catalogue has GND.1, GND.2 and GND.3 and does not say which is which, so I used GND.2. All the GND pins are the same node on the UNO.
The servo is powered from the UNO's 5V pin, within its 4.8-6 V range. Its signal is 5 V logic from pin 9.
The servo's 3-pin connector is modelled as the servo's PWM, V+ and GND ports, each joined to one jumper wire end.
Parts are unchanged from step 1: no breadboard, the SCP1000 breakout is wired directly to the Arduino Uno with 7 hook-up wires (5 blue signal, 1 red 3.3 V, 1 black GND).

Pin mapping follows the schematic and sketch: SCK-D13, MISO-D12, MOSI-D11, CSB-D7, DRDY-D6. In the schematic the DRDY and CSB lines cross, so D7 goes to CSB and D6 goes to DRDY. (The step 1 note describing this was worded confusingly.)
The sensor is powered from the Uno 3.3V pin (red wire), not 5V, because the SCP1000 is a 3.3 V part. GND goes to the Uno's GND pin next to the power header, taken as GND.1.
The SCP1000 breakout's logic pins are connected directly to the Uno's 5V I/O as the tutorial shows, without level shifters. The tutorial does not add any.
Step 1 parts were correct; no parts added or dropped.
No resistor is used: the button is wired between pin 2 and GND and relies on the internal INPUT_PULLUP.

From the image, the button straddles the centre gap in breadboard columns 24 and 25. Side 1 (1.l, 1.r) is in column 24 and side 2 (2.l, 2.r) is in column 25. Pressing the button joins the two columns.
The black wire goes from the Uno GND header pin (next to AREF) to hole 24t.a. The yellow wire goes from Uno pin 2 to hole 25t.a.
The Uno has several GND pins and the image shows the one on the digital header next to AREF. I assumed that is GND.1.
The breadboard hole names map the image's numbered rows to column numbers and its letters to row letters, in the catalogue's '<column><bank>.<row>' scheme.
Parts are unchanged from step 1. All 20 wires and 7 buttons are used in the connections.

The catalogue breadboard has 30 columns, but the image board is wider (about 63) and its buttons are spaced 6 columns apart. I compressed the layout to 4-column spacing so every button fits in columns 1-27. Each button spans columns c and c+2 (c = 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25) across the centre gap. The topology is the same as the image.

Each button's side 1 (1.l and 1.r) is on the bank-b half, and its signal wire joins the strip of its right-hand column. Side 2 (2.l and 2.r) is on the bank-t half. The ground wire goes from that strip to the bn rail, so pressing the button joins the pin to GND. The code uses INPUT_PULLUP, so there are no external resistors.

Rail assignment from the image: the black GND wires go to the rail beside the blue line (tn on top, bn on bottom). The red wires go to the top rail beside the red line (tp). Rail numbers are arbitrary but kept within 1-30.
The Arduino GND wire is assumed to go to GND.1 of the Zero's digital header.

The red IOREF wire goes to tp.28. A second red wire from tp.29 goes to the potentiometer's VCC end. IOREF is 3.3 V on the Zero, which is the pot's supply. The A0 wire goes to the wiper (SIG) and the black wire from the bottom GND rail goes to the pot's GND end, as in the schematic.
The long black wire links the top GND rail to the bottom GND rail. This joins the Arduino GND to the button ground wires and the pot ground.
Jumper wires go directly to the potentiometer's pins, as in the image.

Step 1 was wrong in one place: I added wire21 (Uno GND.2 to the bottom ground rail). The bottom-half B pins and the bottom LED cathodes use the bottom ground rail, and a separate ground feed to it is needed. All other parts are unchanged.

The manual gives no wire layout, so the breadboard positions are my own. The AD5206 sits across the centre gap with pins 1-12 in holes 5t.e to 16t.e, left to right, and pins 24 down to 13 in holes 5b.f to 16b.f. Pin 1 faces pin 24.

All six A pins and VDD go to the +5V rail. A1-A4 are on the bottom half, so their wires run to the top + rail. All six B pins go to ground: B5 and B6 to the top - rail, B1-B4 to the bottom - rail. VSS and the GND pin go to the top - rail. The top - rail and bottom - rail are both fed from Uno ground.
CS goes to Uno pin 10, SDI to pin 11 and CLK to pin 13, as the code comments say.

Each channel's W pin goes through a 220 ohm resistor to the LED anode. The LED cathode goes to a ground rail. Channels 1-6 use led1-led6 and r1-r6. The resistor is on the anode side, as in the schematic.
The wiper (W) is used as the voltage-divider output. The ad5206 part's 'through' pairs model the A-W and W-B resistor tracks, so there are no edges inside the chip.
Bank 'b' rows are f-j and bank 't' rows are a-e. Rail hole numbers are arbitrary, because each rail is one strip.

Fixed the single-use port errors: the MKR ENV Shield is now joined to the MKR WiFi 1010 only through env1:MKR.socket. The jumper wires go to the board's pins (D2-D5, GND), which the shield's headers pass through. I removed the pin-by-pin pass-through edges.

Fixed the resistor count: the parts list has a single '220 ohm' resistor, so r1 is the only one and r2-r4 are removed. I did not give each LED channel its own resistor. Both LED cathodes (white LED and RGB common cathode) go to one shared breadboard strip (column 25), and r1 sits between that strip and the ground rail. That way every LED still has a series current limit with only one resistor. A shared resistor means brightness varies with how many channels are on.
The schematic image was not visible, so the wiring follows the sketch's pin defines: pin 5 is the white LED, pin 2 is RGB red, pin 3 is RGB blue and pin 4 is RGB green.
The MKR ENV Shield (new type, because lookup_part found nothing for it) is stacked on the MKR WiFi 1010. Its temperature sensor is read over internal I2C, which is not drawn as a separate edge.
The breadboard holes used are my own layout choice. The jumper wire count (7) is an assumption.
